To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a temperature increase and an increase of the strain magnitude can result in an increased threshold displacement energy.
the TDE in body-centered cubic (BCC) iron decreases with increasing strain, and it increases with increasing temperature.
the TDE is highly dependent on both temperature and strain.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the determination of the threshold displacement energy of iron under irradiation conditions that are representative of fusion reactor conditions, and thus provides a more accurate prediction of the materials response to neutron irradiation.
the determination of the threshold displacement energy as a function of system temperature and applied stress.
the effect of strain and temperature in determining the threshold displacement energy of bcc iron.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TDE is a function of the strain and temperature.
the TDE is a highly anisotropic quantity that is sensitive to temperature and strain.
the TDE is not constant and varies significantly with applied strain and temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a decrease of strain and temperature results in an increase of TDE.
a temperature increase of 200 K results in an increase of approximately 4 eV in the TDE.
a temperature increase from 0 K to 500K and a strain increase from 0% to 10% results in a decrease in the TDE from 40.5 eV to approximately 30.0 eV.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TDE is a highly variable quantity that must be carefully considered in order to obtain an accurate prediction of the number of displaced atoms.
the TDE is a strong function of strain and system temperature and should be taken into account in any irradiation analysis.
the TDE is highly sensitive to both applied strain and temperature.
